stem: Police question Ben, a suspect in a robbery, without telling him of his right to remain silent and to have a lawyer. Ben then confesses. Under Article III, Section 12 of the 1987 Constitution, what is true of his confession?
choices: It may be used against him if he signs it.
It cannot be used as evidence against him.
It may be used against him if it is true.
It may be used if two officers witnessed it.
answer: It cannot be used as evidence against him.
hints: First ask: did the police follow Section 12? Then ask what Section 12 says happens to a confession taken in breach of it.
The police skipped a duty in Section 12(1): telling Ben of his right to remain silent and to have counsel.
Recall the third paragraph of Section 12, about a confession obtained in violation of it. Then check whether signing, truth or witnesses change that rule.

solution.methodName: Match the situation to the provision

steps.action: Spot the problem: the police did not tell Ben of his right to remain silent and to have a lawyer.
steps.why: These are the first things Section 12 protects. Skipping them is a violation.

steps.action: Section 12(1) says a person under investigation "shall have the right to be informed of his right to remain silent and to have competent and independent counsel". So the questioning broke Section 12.
steps.why: Counsel means a lawyer. Being informed means the police must tell him; he does not have to ask.

steps.action: Section 12(3) says: "Any confession or admission obtained in violation of this or Section 17 hereof shall be inadmissible in evidence against him."
steps.why: "Inadmissible in evidence" means the court cannot accept it as proof.

steps.action: Section 12(3) has no exception for a signed confession, a true confession or witnesses.
steps.why: Section 12(3) asks only one thing: was the confession obtained in violation of Section 12? Here it was.

steps.action: The answer is: it cannot be used as evidence against him.

trapNotes.It may be used against him if he signs i: Signing does not cure the problem. Section 12(3) makes a confession taken in violation of Section 12 "inadmissible in evidence against him".
trapNotes.It may be used against him if it is true: Section 12(3) does not ask whether the confession is true. If it was taken in violation of Section 12, it cannot be used against him.
trapNotes.It may be used if two officers witnessed: Witnesses do not fix the violation. Section 12(3) has no exception for witnesses.
